newsitem.title: UK: Outlook remains uncertain for veg oils - trade.
newsitem.headline: Outlook remains uncertain for veg oils - trade.

text.p: European vegetable oil prices will continue to drift as many players are uncertain over futures market trends.
"It's a very difficult market at the moment, very few people have the confidence to make a positive move," said one trader.

The palm oil market was looking to the PORLA figures on Monday to give that sector some direction, but these proved to be bearish. Malaysia's Palm Oil Registration and Licensing Authority (PORLA) put local end-August stocks at 800,893 tonnes against 755,665 at end-July.
Palm oil output was estimated at 810,550 tonnes up 12.21 percent from July, while exports were 638,601 tonnes against 662,035 tonnes the previous month.
Also on Monday the Malaysian Oil Palm Growers' Council (MOPGC) released an estimate which put local palm oil output in August at 825,000 tonnes, 14.3 percent up from July.

Malaysian cargo surveyor, Societe Generale de Surveillance (SGS) also released figures on Monday which put Malaysian exports during the first 15 days of September at 310,058 tonnes against 287,394 during the same period in August.
So palm oil prices are expected to continue to drift lower, despite recent off-take by India.

Since palm oil prices started to fall in the early part of last week after Pakistan devalued the rupee and cast doubt on its future buying plans, India has bought a total of 24,000 tonnes of palm olein at tenders. But traders do not expect this to continue.
"India is coming to the end of its buying ahead of the local edible oil harvest so we don't expect to see much of them, unless there is a dramatic fall in palm oil prices," said one.
"Another factor is the Indian private sector which seems to have overbought and is now appearing on the market as resellers, adding to the pressure on prices," said another trader.
Traders said the trend for palm oil looks to be lower over the next four months, unless China comes into the market which seems unlikely.
"China is coming into its winter now and they don't buy palm oil that time of year, they tend to go for soft oils," said a trader.
Indonesian palm oil production is also expected to pick up, with traders talking of output of around half a million tonnes a month for the next four months.
And overhanging the whole market is Chicago where the "weather market' is still running, bringing soft oil trading in Europe almost to a standstill.
"Refiners seem quite happy at the moment with their stocks so buyers are not taking positions. In fact most people say they are now going to sit the weather market out," said one trader.
"If we can see a trend developing at all, it's a drift towards a demand-driven business with speculative markets like Chicago being looked on as a side-show," said another trader.
